# Abstract

This settlement gazetteer compiles longitudinal population series for 4.854 catalogued Iraqi cities and towns from the inaugural 1947AD census through the 2024-2025 horizon. Drawn from Iraq's Central Organization for Statistics and Information Technology (COSIT) enumerations of 1947AD, 1957AD, 1965AD, 1977AD, 1987AD and 1997AD alongside 2009AD and 2024AD district estimates, the urban ledger traces a dramatic expansion in aggregate enumerated urban population from 1,47M in 1947AD to 3,84M in 1965AD, 8,22M in 1987AD, 20,69M in 2009AD and 46,84M in 2025AD. Organised across six geographical belts—the Baghdād metropolitan corridor, the northern Kurdistan highlands, the Upper Tigris and Jazīra oil foothills, the Middle Euphrates and Al-Anbār valley, the southern alluvium and marshlands, and the Al-Baṣrah Shatt al-Arab littoral—the tables expose both extreme metropolitan primacy in Baghdād (8,13M peak in 2018AD; 7,95M in 2025AD; Zipf $\alpha = 1{,}303$, $R^2 = 0{,}786$) and sharp local shocks driven by the Iran-Iraq War, Anfal clearances, marshland drainage and post-2003 internal displacement.

# Background

Modern Iraq's urban network grew out of an ancient riverine and caravan geography reordered by twentieth-century oil exports, centralised administration and recurrent warfare. At the inaugural national census of 1947AD, Baghdād already dominated the central Tigris crossing with 515,5k inhabitants across Greater Baghdād, far ahead of the northern caravan and administrative centre of Al-Mawṣil (133,6k), the southern Gulf port of Al-Baṣrah (101,5k), the oil-boom railhead of Kirkūk (68,3k) and the Kurdish piedmont cities of As-Sulaymāniyah (33,5k) and Arbīl (27k). Throughout the middle decades of the twentieth century, landlessness in the southern riverain provinces, state investment in flood-control barrages and the rapid growth of public-sector employment accelerated rural-to-urban migration into Baghdād, Kirkūk and Al-Baṣrah [@Wojtaszek2025Isolated; @Anonymous2017Case].

Between 1980 and 2017, conflict and environmental disruption repeatedly altered urban growth trajectories across provinces. Artillery shelling along the Shatt al-Arab during the Iran-Iraq War temporarily hollowed out Al-Baṣrah and southern river ports [@Lorenz2013Strategic], while the 1987-1988 Anfal campaign razed upland Kurdish villages and drove rural families into collective towns around Arbīl, As-Sulaymāniyah and Dahūk [@Ahram2023There; @Romano2007Refugee]. During the 1990s, international sanctions eroded living standards in Baghdād [@Wojtaszek2025Isolated; @Wang2017Global], and state drainage canals desiccated the southern Al-Ahwār marshes, forcing tens of thousands of *Ma'dān* households into An-Nāṣiriyah, Al-'Amārah and Baghdād's eastern districts [@Znad2024Conflicts; @Yldrm2023Torn]. Later, the 2003-2011 war and the 2014-2017 Islamic State occupation displaced millions from Al-Mawṣil, Ar-Ramādī, Al-Fallūjah and Tikrīt toward Baghdād, Karbalā', An-Najaf and Kurdistan before post-2017 reconstruction reopened northern and western urban cores [@Cetorelli2014Effect; @Sharara2021Health; @Koush2024Heritage].

# Methodology

Every settlement included in this gazetteer derives from COSIT national population censuses (1947-1997) harmonised with 2009AD listing frames and 2024AD district-level urban estimates across official census and projection horizons from 1947AD to 2025AD. Out of 5.104 candidate localities screened in the regional source ledger, 4.854 distinct urban and town centres passed deduplication and boundary separation rules, whereas 250 duplicate aliases and contiguous suburban towns were excluded or merged into canonical parent cities to prevent double-counting. Where original municipal registers record Arabic-script names, tables display standardised Latin romanisations with scholarly diacritics so that every toponym renders cleanly without missing-glyph substitutions.

To reflect Iraq's physical and administrative geography, the 4.854 settlements are partitioned into six contiguous zones ordered from the national capital outward: (1) Baghdād Metropolitan Corridor and Lower Diyālā (456 centres); (2) Kurdistan Highlands and Garmiyan Piedmont across Arbīl, As-Sulaymāniyah, Dahūk and Ḥalabjah (1453 centres); (3) Upper Tigris, Jazīra and Kirkūk Foothills across Nīnawā, Kirkūk and Ṣalāḥ ad-Dīn (976 centres); (4) Middle Euphrates, Al-Anbār and Wāsiṭ (1093 centres); (5) Southern Alluvium and Marshland Edge across Dhī Qār, Maysān, Al-Qādisiyyah and Al-Muthannā (732 centres); and (6) Al-Baṣrah and the Shatt al-Arab Littoral (144 centres). Within each regional table, settlements are ranked in descending order by peak population across five benchmark columns (1947AD, 1965AD, 1987AD, 2009AD and 2025AD), with hyphens marking benchmarks where a smaller town was not separately enumerated.

# Testing and Validation

Cross-checking the 4.854 urban trajectories against Iraq's 88 geoBoundaries second-order administrative districts (qadhas) [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] confirms tight structural alignment between municipal growth and subadministrative census enumerations. Across the full sample, peak settlement sizes obey a steep Zipf rank-size power law ($\alpha = 1{,}303$, $R^2 = 0{,}786$), capturing Baghdād's commanding lead over Al-Mawṣil while accommodating a broad tail of district towns and smaller provincial centres. Table \ref{tab:excluded-suburbs} summarises the 250 excluded duplicate aliases and merged suburban localities screened out during ledger deduplication.

## Baghdād Metropolitan Corridor and Lower Diyālā

Table \ref{tab:zone1-baghdad} records 456 settlements anchoring the central Tigris-Diyālā core, led by Baghdād (8,13M peak in 2018AD; 7,95M in 2025AD) and the Diyālā provincial capital of Ba'qūbah (467,9k peak in 2003AD; 391k in 2025AD), together with fast-growing peri-urban satellites such as Abū Ghraib, Al-Waḥdah, Al-Maḥmūdiyah, Al-Muqdādiyah and Al-Khāliṣ [@Wojtaszek2025Isolated].

## Kurdistan Highlands and Garmiyan Piedmont

Table \ref{tab:zone2-kurdistan} covers 1453 cities and towns across Arbīl, As-Sulaymāniyah, Dahūk and the Garmiyan piedmont. Rapid post-1991 institutional stability and refugee return [@Romano2007Refugee; @Hamelink2025Enacting] propelled Arbīl to 1,02M, As-Sulaymāniyah to an 878,1k peak in 2018AD (840,5k in 2025AD), Dahūk to 459,4k and border-trade hub Zākhū to 301,4k by 2025AD.

## Upper Tigris, Jazīra and Kirkūk Foothills

Table \ref{tab:zone3-north} enumerates 976 settlements across Nīnawā, Kirkūk and Ṣalāḥ ad-Dīn, headed by Al-Mawṣil (1,8M peak in 2008AD; 1,55M in 2025AD), the oil metropolis of Kirkūk (1,27M), Sāmarrā' (348,7k peak in 2003AD), Tikrīt (260k peak in 2002AD) and Tal'afar (181k) [@Anonymous2017Case; @Koush2024Heritage].

## Middle Euphrates, Al-Anbār and Wāsiṭ

Table \ref{tab:zone4-mideuphrates} spans 1093 centres across the Euphrates valley and central irrigation plains, anchored by Ar-Ramādī (874,5k peak in 2005AD; 299,3k in 2025AD), the shrine cities of An-Najaf (842,4k) and Karbalā' (795,3k), Al-Ḥillah (541k peak in 2015AD; 477,6k in 2025AD), Tigris agricultural hub Al-Kūt (513,2k) and Al-Fallūjah (312,8k) [@Cetorelli2014Effect; @Diwakar2019Violent].

## Southern Alluvium and Marshland Edge

Table \ref{tab:zone5-south} documents 732 settlements across Dhī Qār, Maysān, Al-Qādisiyyah and Al-Muthannā, led by An-Nāṣiriyah (860,2k peak in 2012AD; 714,9k in 2025AD), Al-'Amārah (677,8k), Ad-Dīwāniyah (401,8k) and As-Samāwah (260,3k), reflecting decades of rural migration off drained marshlands and salinised paddies [@Znad2024Conflicts; @Mamshai2023Climate].

# Limitations

Three evidentiary constraints shape these urban series. First, while major provincial capitals preserve continuous COSIT census series from 1947AD through 1987AD, smaller secondary and district towns entered national registers only in later enumerations (2003AD, 2009AD or 2015AD), marked by hyphens in earlier benchmark columns. Second, the exclusion of Arbīl, As-Sulaymāniyah and Dahūk from the 1997AD national census and the 27-year hiatus prior to November 2024 mean that post-1990 urban curves blend civil-registry ration-frame counts with 2009AD and 2024AD district estimates [@Romano2007Refugee; @Mansour2023Iraq]. Third, continuous suburban sprawl along the margins of Baghdād, Al-Baṣrah and Arbīl blurs municipal boundaries between core urban rings and newly incorporated satellite townships.

# Conclusion

From the 1947AD census through 2025AD, Iraq's 4.854 catalogued settlements grew from 1,47M enumerated urban inhabitants to 46,84M in 2025AD while preserving a steep primate hierarchy ($\alpha = 1{,}303$, $R^2 = 0{,}786$) anchored by Baghdād (8,13M peak; 7,95M in 2025AD). Despite severe wartime shocks along the Shatt al-Arab, northern Kurdish valleys, the southern marshes and the Upper Tigris corridor, sustained high fertility [@Cetorelli2014Effect] and rural-to-urban migration drove rapid expansion across every tier of Iraqi cities and provincial towns.
